docs.title: Emanuele Marchetti
docs.text:
For sixteen years I talked to the machine. Now I talk to people.

Four real problems, explained by someone who has been on both sides of them.

docs.title: The purchasing process stops without providing an explanation. Just a blank page
docs.text:
Applies to: Web checkout, customer account portal Level: Beginner Time to resolve: 5–10 minutes

You select a digital service, correctly proceed to checkout, and press the purchase button. The page turns blank.

Nothing is broken, and no payment has been taken. The checkout is just missing information.

docs.title: Why this happens
docs.text:
When you select checkout, the system retrieves the selected item, your payment method, and your account information. Your account information must be complete before the transaction can proceed, and this typically includes an address and a phone number, not only a name and an email address.

The checkout process does not validate whether these fields are present. When they are missing, the transaction stops, but no error is returned and no message is displayed. The result is a blank page.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Make sure your cart contains at least one item and that you are logged in to your account. These two conditions account for a significant percentage of similar cases.

If you have not updated your browser in some time, update it before continuing. An outdated browser can produce the same blank page for a different reason.

docs.title: Step 1: Check that your profile is complete
docs.text:
Open the profile section of your account and confirm that every required field is filled in, in particular your address and phone number. A name and an email address are not sufficient.

Complete any missing fields, save, and attempt the purchase again.

If the purchase completes, you are finished. If not, continue.

docs.title: Step 2: Clear your browser cache
docs.text:
Your browser may be holding an outdated copy of the checkout page. Clear the cache, or open the site in a private window, and attempt the purchase once more.

If the purchase completes, you are finished. If not, the cause lies elsewhere. Continue.

docs.title: Step 3: Rule out account and consent issues
docs.text:
Confirm that you have accepted the current terms of use, and that you are signed in to a single account. Registering more than once with different email addresses can leave you signed in to an account that does not hold your completed profile.

If the purchase still fails, the problem is not one of the common causes, and it needs to be reported.

docs.title: If it still fails
docs.text:
Collect the following before contacting support. It will save a round trip:

  • The device you used, desktop or mobile
  • Your browser and its version
  • The date and time of your last attempt
  • A screenshot of the page you see

Written by Emanuele Marchetti

docs.title: You moved a number into the destination, but the destination does not hold a number
docs.text:
Applies to: COBOL packed-decimal fields (COMP-3) Level: Intermediate

You moved a number from one field to another. It should remain the same, but after the move, you see something different. There are no other operations to check. Just the MOVE.

The data is still the same. It looks different now, because of the format.

docs.title: Why this happens
docs.text:
COMP-3 stores a number in packed form: two digits share each byte, and the last half-byte holds the sign. The number 12345 occupies three bytes rather than five.

This works as long as the field is treated as what it is, a number. If you move it into an alphanumeric field, COBOL does not convert it. The bytes are copied as they are, and read as characters they mean nothing.

docs.title: Why odd and even behave differently
docs.text:
A byte holds two digits, and the sign always takes half a byte at the end.

Declare five digits and the field fits exactly: five digits plus the sign make three full bytes. Declare six, and there is half a byte left over at the front. COBOL ignores it in calculations, but copies it along with everything else.

docs.title: If you need to read the value
docs.text: Move the field into a numeric DISPLAY field, not an alphanumeric one. COBOL unpacks the digits and writes one per byte, and the value appears as a number.

docs.title: If you need to move the bytes
docs.text: Copying a COMP-3 field into an alphanumeric field preserves the bytes, not the value. The field cannot be read, compared, or used in arithmetic. This is acceptable when the bytes are being written to a file or passed to another program that knows how to interpret them. It is not a way to inspect the data.

docs.title: Declare an odd number of digits
docs.text:
A COMP-3 field declared with an odd number of digits fills its bytes exactly. Declared with an even number, it carries half a byte that nothing initialises and nothing clears. Choosing an odd number removes the problem entirely.

Written by Emanuele Marchetti

docs.title: LEFT JOIN: why your rows disappear when you filter in the WHERE clause
The rule
docs.text: In a LEFT JOIN, a condition on the optional side of the join belongs in the ON clause, not the WHERE clause.

docs.title: The scenario
docs.text: You need a complete list of names from the Authors table and any corresponding books from the Books table, pairing authors with books, but including only titles from 1957.

docs.title: The query that looks correct
docs.text:
This is the query we would probably write. It looks valid, but it does not return the results you want.

SELECT a.name, b.title
FROM authors a
LEFT JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id
WHERE b.year = 1957;
name title Calvino Il barone rampante

docs.title: The result
docs.text: The result is a shorter list that does not include every author; the authors who are present all have at least one book from 1957. The WHERE clause filtered out the rows that would have displayed authors with no books from 1957.

docs.title: The reason
docs.text: It is a matter of sequence. The WHERE clause comes into play after the query has already generated an initial list containing authors who do not have books from 1957. It operates on that list, removing rows for authors where the publication year value is missing because, effectively, NULL does not satisfy the condition = 1957.

docs.title: The solution
docs.text:
Therefore, the condition needs to be moved earlier in the sequence; this can be done by using the ON clause, which operates at the JOIN level, and thus prior to the WHERE clause. With this syntax, authors who do not have a corresponding book written in 1957 remain in the list rather than being discarded later.

SELECT a.name, b.title
FROM authors a
LEFT JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id AND b.year = 1957;
name title Calvino Il barone rampante Ginzburg NULL Levi NULL Morante NULL

docs.title: You asked for a list, you got a list. It does not tell you how many there are.
docs.text:
You called the API and it gave you exactly the list you expected. Now you base your work on it.

How many stations are there really?

In this list you know what's there, not what isn't.

There is a cap on the number of stations in the response; it is called limit.

When there are more stations than the limit, you receive exactly limit stations. The rest is left out. No alert.

You cannot tell whether you have a complete list or one that just reached the limit.

Request the list one page at a time. As long as a page comes back full, you request the next. When a page comes back with fewer, you can assume you have reached the end.

Exactly. You asked for stations, and that is what you got. But you wanted all of them.
